explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, shouts, "Every man to his tent, O Israel!" (2 Samuel 20:1). It's the old "I'm out, everybody grab your coats" move. One shout, and he's asking a whole crowd to head for the door.

Sheba does stir up trouble, but his words aren't a fight call. He says, "Every man to his tent, O Israel!" (2 Samuel 20:1). Tents are where you go when you're leaving, not when you're swinging. His shout is about walking away from David.

I get why you'd think so, since a man blowing a horn sure sounds like a man who wants a crown. But his shout never mentions one. He says, "We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse's son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!" (2 Samuel 20:1). The call is to leave David, and the men of Israel do follow Sheba afterward.

Yep. "All the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri" (2 Samuel 20:2). I've been left in a drawer before, and I'm telling you, that kind of leaving stings. David's whole crowd just turned and walked.

Judah is the group that stays. The text says the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 20:2). So when the horn sounds, Israel walks off and Judah stays put. Flip those two and you've got the whole verse backwards.

The mighty men don't desert. In the very next scene they march out of Jerusalem to chase Sheba (2 Samuel 20:7). The ones who deserted are the men of Israel (2 Samuel 20:2). The mighty men stay on David's side of the line.

True! "But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem" (2 Samuel 20:2). While everybody else is heading for the exits, Judah stays right with David. That's a long walk to make beside him.

This one is true, friend. The text says the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 20:2). It's Israel's men who leave to follow Sheba. Judah stays on the road with David the whole way.

That's the word. David puts the ten concubines in a house under guard and provides for them, and they live as widows until the day they die (2 Samuel 20:3). I think this is one of the heavy parts of the chapter. It's hard to read, and it's okay to sit with that for a second.
No crowns in this verse. The ten concubines are placed in a house under guard, and they live as widows (2 Samuel 20:3). I think this is a heavy moment, and nothing in it looks like royal treatment.

Close, but the text uses a different word. David provides for them, but he no longer sleeps with them, and they're confined until the day of their death, living as widows (2 Samuel 20:3). I think this part of the story is a heavy one. It calls them widows, not servants.

Three days, right on the money. David says, "Summon the men of Judah to come to me within three days, and be here yourself" (2 Samuel 20:4). Amasa, the man David told to gather Judah, gets a short, clear deadline. Three days is plenty to set a few alarms.

Seven would be a more relaxed week. David's actual deadline is tighter. He tells Amasa, the man he sends to gather Judah, to come "within three days" (2 Samuel 20:4). Three days, and the clock is already ticking.

Forty days? Friend, that's not a deadline, that's a season. David tells Amasa, the man he sends to gather Judah, to come "within three days" (2 Samuel 20:4). With a rebellion going, he can't wait around for forty.
Not this time, friend. The text says Amasa "took longer than the time allotted him" (2 Samuel 20:5). David gave him three days, and Amasa runs over. The King can't wait, so he looks to someone else.

False is right. Amasa goes to summon Judah, but he takes longer than the time allotted him (2 Samuel 20:5). We've all been the one saying "almost there" while the clock keeps going. I'll be honest, I've done that with a batch or two myself.

That's what David fears. He tells Abishai, Joab's brother, to pursue Sheba "or he will find fortified cities and elude us" (2 Samuel 20:6). Walled cities are hard to get into. So David wants Sheba caught before he can get behind one.

David doesn't mention allies from other lands. His worry is that Sheba "will find fortified cities and elude us" (2 Samuel 20:6). He's talking to Abishai, Joab's brother. His fear is walls Sheba could slip behind.

Caves would make a fine hideout, but that's not what David says. He tells Abishai, Joab's brother, to move fast "or he will find fortified cities and elude us" (2 Samuel 20:6). The danger is Sheba getting behind city walls.

True, and that's what makes it so chilling. Joab, who was over David's army (2 Samuel 20:23), asks Amasa, "Are you well, my brother?" and takes him by the beard to kiss him (2 Samuel 20:9). All that while the dagger is already out of its sheath (2 Samuel 20:8). It sounds friendly, and that's the danger of it.

The greeting does happen, friend. Joab has already slipped his dagger from its sheath (2 Samuel 20:8). Then he asks Amasa, "Are you well, my brother?" and grabs him by the beard with his right hand to kiss him (2 Samuel 20:9). Amasa isn't on guard against the dagger in Joab's hand (2 Samuel 20:10).

Yes. Joab stabs Amasa in the stomach, and he doesn't need to strike again, for Amasa is dead (2 Samuel 20:10). I think this is one of the hardest parts of the chapter. It's heavy, and it's okay that it feels that way.

Nobody stops him. After Amasa falls, the text says Joab and his brother Abishai pursue Sheba (2 Samuel 20:10). I think this is a heavy part to read. Amasa is not on guard, and Joab doesn't need a second strike.

There's no struggle in the text. Amasa "was not on guard against the dagger in Joab's hand," and Joab stabbed him (2 Samuel 20:10). He's dead without a second blow. I think this is a heavy moment, and the text tells it plainly.

They stop. The text says the man "saw that all the troops were stopping there" while Amasa lay in the middle of the road (2 Samuel 20:12). A whole army is halted by what they see. Then the young man drags the body off the road and throws a garment over it.

The text doesn't say anyone weeps. It says the young man saw that all the troops were stopping there (2 Samuel 20:12). Then he drags the body off the road into a field and throws a garment over it. I think it's a quiet, stunned moment, but that's me guessing.

They don't scatter. The text says the troops stop where Amasa lies (2 Samuel 20:12). Only after the body is moved from the road do the men go on with Joab (2 Samuel 20:13). So the army pauses, then keeps going.

True. The young man drags the body into a field and throws a garment over it, and "as soon as Amasa's body was removed from the road, all the men went on with Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri" (2 Samuel 20:12-13). The road is clear and the chase is back on. Nobody is standing around anymore.

This one is true. The body gets moved off the road, and the text says all the men then went on with Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri (2 Samuel 20:13). The army was stopped, and once the road was clear, everybody follows Joab.

That's the one. Joab's troops besiege Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah (2 Samuel 20:15). Sheba had passed through all the tribes of Israel to get there (2 Samuel 20:14). That's a mouthful of a name, and it's where the chase ends.

Gibeon is where the great stone is, and where Amasa catches up with the army (2 Samuel 20:8). It's not where Sheba is trapped. The text says Joab's troops besiege him in Abel-beth-maacah (2 Samuel 20:15).
Mahanaim isn't the city in this passage. The text says Joab's troops besieged Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah (2 Samuel 20:15). That's where Sheba ends up.

True. The troops build a siege ramp against the outer rampart, and all of them are "battering the wall to topple it" (2 Samuel 20:15). That's an army that came to work. It's a lot of hammering on one city wall.

This one is true, friend. After the troops build the siege ramp, the text says they were all "battering the wall to topple it" (2 Samuel 20:15). They aren't just standing there looking at the wall. They're hard at work on it.

A wise woman it is. She calls out from the city, "Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him" (2 Samuel 20:16). The text never gives her name. All it says is that she's wise, and her words end up settling the whole matter.
The text doesn't call her a prophet. It says "a wise woman called out from the city" (2 Samuel 20:16). She asks for Joab by name and says she wants to speak with him. Wise is the word the text picks.
Elders do show up in Scripture, but not here. The text says "a wise woman called out from the city" (2 Samuel 20:16). She wants to speak with Joab, and he does end up listening.

explanations.answer: Why he would swallow up the LORD's inheritance
explanations.explanation: Right, and that's a sharp question. She asks, "Why would you swallow up the LORD's inheritance?" (2 Samuel 20:19). She says she's among the peaceable and faithful in Israel, and that her city is "a mother in Israel." She doesn't shout back at the army. She asks a question.

explanations.answer: Why he would break his oath to the king
explanations.explanation: No oath comes up here. Her question is, "Why would you swallow up the LORD's inheritance?" (2 Samuel 20:19). She's talking about the city itself, which she calls "a mother in Israel." The question is about the city, not about any oath.

explanations.answer: Why he would defy the word of the king
explanations.explanation: She says nothing about the king's word. She asks Joab, "Why would you swallow up the LORD's inheritance?" (2 Samuel 20:19). She's speaking up for her city, which she calls "a mother in Israel." That's the heart of her question.

That's the deal. Joab says Sheba son of Bichri has lifted up his hand against the king, and tells her, "Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city" (2 Samuel 20:21). He wants one man, not the whole city. That's a pretty short list of demands.
Joab never asks for the gates. He says, "Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city" (2 Samuel 20:21). The "him" is Sheba. Joab wants only that one man handed over.
No gold is mentioned. Joab's request is, "Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city" (2 Samuel 20:21). The man he wants is Sheba. That's all Joab asks for.

Not alive, friend. The woman says, "Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall" (2 Samuel 20:21). I think this is a heavy part of the story, and the text says it plainly. The people of the city then do what she says (2 Samuel 20:22).

False is right. She tells Joab, "Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall" (2 Samuel 20:21). I think this is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't soften it. She promises his head, not a man handed over alive.

explanations.answer: Each go to their own home
explanations.explanation: Yep. Joab blows the ram's horn, and his men disperse from the city, "each to his own home" (2 Samuel 20:22). The same kind of horn that started the rebellion now ends the siege. The army goes home, and the wall is still standing.

explanations.answer: March in and take the city
explanations.explanation: They don't go in. When Joab blows the ram's horn, his men disperse from the city, each to his own home (2 Samuel 20:22). Joab had said he would depart if Sheba was delivered (2 Samuel 20:21). The army leaves the city standing.

The Berites do show up in this chapter. They gathered together and followed Sheba (2 Samuel 20:14). But the text doesn't send the army after them. After Joab's horn, his men disperse from the city, each to his own home (2 Samuel 20:22).

True. The text says, "And Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem" (2 Samuel 20:22). The chase that began with one horn ends with Joab walking back to David. This is the last stretch of Absalom's whole story.
This one is true, friend. After the horn and the men going home, "Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem" (2 Samuel 20:22). The soldiers each go to their own homes, and Joab goes back to David.
